title: Monitoring bird migration with a fixed-beam radar and a thermal-imaging camera
abstract: Previous studies using thermal imaging cameras (TI) have used target size as an indicator of target altitude when radar was not available, but this approach may lead to errors if birds that differ greatly in size are actually ﬂying at the same altitude. To overcome this potential difﬁculty and obtain more accurate measures of the ﬂight altitudes and numbers of individual migrants, we have developed a technique that combines a vertically pointed stationary radar beam and a vertically pointed thermal imaging camera (VERTRAD/TI). The TI provides accurate counts of the birds passing through a ﬁxed, circular sampling area in the TI display, and the radar provides accurate data on their ﬂight altitudes. We analyzed samples of VERTRAD/TI video data collected during nocturnal fall migration in 2000 and 2003 and during the arrival of spring trans-Gulf migration during the daytime in 2003. We used a video peak store (VPS) to make time exposures of target tracks in the video record of the TI and developed criteria to distinguish birds, foraging bats, and insects based on characteristics of the tracks in the VPS images and the altitude of the targets. The TI worked equally well during daytime and nighttime observations and best when skies were clear, because thermal radiance from cloud heat often obscured targets. The VERTRAD/TI system, though costly, is a valuable tool for measuring accurate bird migration trafﬁc rates (the number of birds crossing 1609.34 m [1 statute mile] of front per hour) for different altitudinal strata above 25 m. The technique can be used to estimate the potential risk of migrating birds colliding with man-made obstacles of various heights (e.g., communication and broadcast towers and wind turbines)—a subject of increasing importance to conservation biologists.

# **Monitoring bird migration with a fixed-beam radar and a thermal-imaging camera**

Sidney A. Gauthreaux, Jr.[1] and John W. Livingston

_Department of Biological Sciences, Clemson University, Clemson, South Carolina 29634-0314, USA_ Received 30 June 2005; accepted 2 May 2006

ABSTRACT. Previous studies using thermal imaging cameras (TI) have used target size as an indicator of target altitude when radar was not available, but this approach may lead to errors if birds that differ greatly in size are actually flying at the same altitude. To overcome this potential difficulty and obtain more accurate measures of the flight altitudes and numbers of individual migrants, we have developed a technique that combines a vertically pointed stationary radar beam and a vertically pointed thermal imaging camera (VERTRAD/TI). The TI provides accurate counts of the birds passing through a fixed, circular sampling area in the TI display, and the radar provides accurate data on their flight altitudes. We analyzed samples of VERTRAD/TI video data collected during nocturnal fall migration in 2000 and 2003 and during the arrival of spring trans-Gulf migration during the daytime in 2003. We used a video peak store (VPS) to make time exposures of target tracks in the video record of the TI and developed criteria to distinguish birds, foraging bats, and insects based on characteristics of the tracks in the VPS images and the altitude of the targets. The TI worked equally well during daytime and nighttime observations and best when skies were clear, because thermal radiance from cloud heat often obscured targets. The VERTRAD/TI system, though costly, is a valuable tool for measuring accurate bird migration traffic rates (the number of birds crossing 1609.34 m [1 statute mile] of front per hour) for different altitudinal strata above 25 m. The technique can be used to estimate the potential risk of migrating birds colliding with man-made obstacles of various heights (e.g., communication and broadcast towers and wind turbines)—a subject of increasing importance to conservation biologists.

## SINOPSIS. **Monitoreo de aves migratorias con radar de rayos fijos y una c ́amara de imagen termal**

Estudios previos, en donde no se ha hecho uso de radar, han utilizado c ́amaras infrarojas de imagen termal (CIT) y el tama ̃no de individuos como indicador, para detereminar la altura de vuelo. Sin embargo, este m ́etodo puede dar origen a errores si las aves que vuelan a una misma altura var ́ıan en tama ̃no. Para subsanar esta dificultad y tomar medidas m ́as exactas de la altura de vuelo y el n ́umero de individuos en una bandada, desarrollamos una t ́ecnica que combina un radar de rayos fijos con antena parab ́olica (RRF) con una c ́amara infraroja de imagen termal (RRT/CIT). El CIT provee de un conteo preciso de las aves pasando por un  ́area circular fija de muestreo y el radar provee el dato preciso de la altura de vuelo. Utilizando una videograbadora digital, analizamos las muestras tomadas con la combinaci ́on RRT/CIT durante la migraci ́on oto ̃nal noctura en el 2000 y el 2003 y durante la migraci ́on primaveral diurna del 2003, a trav ́es del Golfo de M ́exico. Utilizamos la c ́amara de video para hacer exposiciones en lapsos de tiempo en lo tomado por el CIT y desarrollamos criterios para distinguir entre aves, murci ́elagos e insectos, usando la huella dejada en el video y la altura del objeto. El CIT trabajo de forma eficiente tanto de dia como de noche, pero a ́un mejor cuando el cielo estaba despejado (cuando esta ausente la interferencia por la irradiaci ́on de calor de parte de las nubes). El sistema RRT/CIT, aunque costoso, es una herramienta valiosa para medir con presici ́on las rutas migratorias y el n ́umero de aves movi ́endose a diferente altura. Dicho sistema es de gran utilidad para determinar el riesgo de coliciones de aves migratorias con obst ́aculos construidos por el hombre a diferentes alturas (ej. torres de comunicaci ́on o turbinas de viento), asuntos de gran relevancia e importancia para la conservaci ́on de aves.

_Key words:_ flight altitude, migration, migration traffic rate, radar, thermal imager

Direct visual studies of nocturnal bird migration have historically been conducted using binoculars or a telescope either by viewing silhouettes of birds crossing the face of the moon (moon-watching technique; Lowery 1951, Lowery and Newman 1955, Newman 1956) or viewing birds (illuminated from the

1Corresponding author. Email: sagth@clemson.edu

ground) passing through a narrow, vertical light beam with binoculars, telescope (ceilometer technique; Gauthreaux 1969), or an image intensifier (Gauthreaux 1979). Although moonwatching is better than the ceilometer technique for discriminating birds, bats, and insects aloft, moon-watching is restricted to a few nights around the full moon without clouds, and vertical light beams may influence the flight behavior of targets on nights when the light beam is clearly

visible because of high atmospheric humidity. During daylight hours, a cloudless blue sky and haze may make it nearly impossible to detect high flying migrants by direct visual observation. To overcome these shortcomings, more recent visual studies of migration have incorporated passive infrared (IR) cameras (Buurma 1988, Winkelman 1992, Bruderer and Liechti 1994) that detect the heat generated by a target. These cameras make it possible to distinguish among birds, insects, and foraging bats (Zehnder et al. 2001). However, none of these techniques provides accurate information on the distance to target or altitude of flight.

Liechti et al. (1995) found that the proportion of birds detected by tracking radar and thermal imager (TI) did not change with distance between 0.5 and 3 km, and the “very rough grouping of birds into three size classes by moonwatchers and IR-operators is closely related to the distances measured by the tracking radar.” Subsequent investigators (Fortin et al. 1999, Zehnder et al. 2001) have used the relationship between silhouette size and distance to group targets into various height classes when a TI is not used with radar. However, if many differentsized birds are migrating and target size is used to estimate height, then targets of different size (e.g., a warbler and a heron) flying at the same altitude will be classified as flying at different heights.

Migration traffic rate (MTR, the number of birds crossing a mile of front [1609.34 m] per hour) is a standard metric of bird migration studies. Using a “very rough grouping of birds into three size classes” to estimate altitude does not permit accurate determination of MTRs because the altitude of individual birds is unknown. For accurate measures of MTRs, accurate information about the altitudes of birds crossing the vertical field of view is needed because sample space increases with altitude. Highresolution radar with a fixed, narrow, vertically pointing beam provides accurate measures of target altitude (Blokpoel 1971). Here, we report on a technique that combines vertically pointing, fixed-conical beam radar with a vertically pointing thermal imager (VERTRAD/TI). This approach (VERTRAD/TI) simultaneously provides information on the altitude and flight direction of each individual bird (and flock), and the information can be used to compute MTRs for different altitudinal strata. Because

this technique can be used during day and night, daytimeandnighttimeMTRscanbecompared.

## **METHODS**

> **Equipment.** The TI (Radiance 1, Amber Raytheon, Goleta, CA) is an IR camera system with a full screen resolution of 640 × 482 pixels. The detector frame rate is 60/s. With a 100-mm lens, the field of view is 5.57[◦] (horizontal screen dimension) and 4.19[◦] (vertical screen dimension). We pointed the TI camera up a vertically pointing, narrow radar beam and oriented the TI so the top of the field of view was aligned toward north (Fig. 1A). The TI detected the path of a target ( _X_ and _Y_ dimensions) and the radar detected its altitude ( _Z_ dimension).

We used marine radar (Pathfinder Model 3400, Raytheon Inc., Manchester, NH) and replaced the typical open array antenna with a parabolic antenna (61-cm diameter) that produced a beam width of 4[◦] . The vertically pointing antenna sat on top of a transmitterreceiver unit connected to a display unit (178-mm cathode ray tube) and rectifier by cables. The transmitter frequency was 9410 ± 30 MHz (3-cm wavelength) with a peak power output of 5 kW and a minimum range of detection of 25 m. At night, our settings were a 2778 m (1.5 nautical mile) range, a pulse length of 0.08 s/3000 Hz pulse repetition frequency (range resolution of 12 m), and range marks every 463 m. During the day, we used a 5556 m (3.0 nautical mile) range, a pulse length of 0.35 s/1500 Hz pulse repetition frequency (range resolution of 52.5 m), and range marks every 926 m. We used different settings for night and day because trans-Gulf migrants arriving at the Gulf Coast typically fly higher during the day than at night (Gauthreaux 1972).

To combine information from the TI camera and the vertical radar display into a single video display, we configured components as shown in Figure 1B. The Radiance I thermal-imaging camera and the camera recording the radar beam (Model TRV-17; Sony Digital Handycam, Sony Electronics Inc., Park Ridge, NJ) were synchronized by the splitter (Model PXD310E; PIX/2 DSP Split Screen/Fader, MicroImage Video Systems,Boyertown,PA),withtheoutputgoingtoa date/timegenerator(ModelMCG-2;BurstElectronic Inc., Albuquerque, NM) then to a miniDV recorder (Model GV-D300, Sony Video

Walkman, Sony Electronics Inc.), and lastly to a WG 14 B/W video monitor (Hitachi Kokusai Electric, Inc., Woodbury, NY).

**Data collection.** We collected data at Pendleton, South Carolina (34[◦] 39[′] N, 82[◦] 47[′] W), during the evening of 26–27 September 2000, and at Wallops Island, Virginia (37[◦] 53[′] N, 75[◦] 30[′] W), about 6 km south of the Wallops Island Flight Facility (NASA) on nine dates in 2003 (16 October–3 November) when weather conditions (no rain and relatively clear skies) allowed data collection. Daylight observations were made on 1 May 2003 at McFaddin National Wildlife Refuge, Texas (29[◦] 40[′] N, 94[◦] 04[′] W).

**Data analysis.** We used a Model 443 video peak store (VPS; Colorado Video Inc., Boulder, CO) to analyze the video tapes. This device stores pixels in a new video frame if they are brighter than the corresponding pixels already stored in frame memory and, over time, a light target moving against a dark background produces a bright track (Figs. 2A–D). We analyzed these tracks using the following criteria: (1) bright targets showing a straight track with modulation along the track (from wing-beat patterns) in the VPS and echo modulation in the vertical radar beam were classified as birds (Figs. 2A and B), (2) gray and dull targets with no visible modulation along the VPS track and no modulation in the vertical radar beam or targets appearing as circles in the VPS with no echo in the radar beam were as

insects (Fig. 2C), and (3) bright targets showing tracks with sharp turns and occasional pauses with little modulation in the VPS track and echo modulation in the vertical radar beam were classified as bats (Fig. 2D). Because the direction of target movement is not evident in a completed VPS track (time exposure), it is important to note the direction of target movement while generating a VPS track. With multiple targets, it is also difficult to associate the altitude of a target with its track in the completed VPS image (e.g., Fig. 2D), and track-altitude associations should be noted as VPS images are being generated.

For data collected on 26–27 September 2000, we analyzed 5-min samples every 15 min from 00:00 to 03:00 UTC. For data collected during the spring of 2003, we analyzed 5-min samples every 15 min from 20:40 to 23:58 UTC. We used the VPS to extract every track in a 5-min sample of the video record and determined the altitude of the target’s echo in the radar beam (if present), the direction of flight, and identity of the target using the above criteria. Data were then entered into a spreadsheet along with date and time. Similarly, we analyzed two 5-min samples taken from 23:25 to 23:30 UTC and from 00:25 to 00:30 UTC on each of nine nights from 16 October to 3 November 2003. These times were chosen because winds aloft was also being measured at the same time, and wind data were needed to discriminate bird echoes from insect echoes recorded by two types of surveillance radar in another study. To determine the number of birds crossing the 1609.34 m migration front, we computed and applied correction factors to each bird based on its altitude because the sample area of the beam increased with altitude. We then corrected the total number of birds for time sampled to generate the rate of passage per hour. We first computed MTRs for all birds at all altitudes and then did so for only birds above a 60-m altitudinal threshold. This allowed us to contrast theamountofmigrationbetween25and60m(a stratum with many man-made obstructions such as communication towers and wind turbines) with that above 60 m. Although the TI detected bird targets below 25 m, these were not included in our MTR calculations because we did not know the exact altitude of these detections. In our analyses of MTR and altitudinal distribution, only targets detected by both VERTRAD and TI were used.

## **RESULTS**

**Night monitoring, fall 2000 and 2003.** The VERTRAD/TI system readily detected birds, bats, and insects (Table 1), with 35–94% of detections identified as birds. Eleven of 17 detections were insects and six were birds on 16– 17 October 2003, and 17 of 26 detections were insects and nine were birds on 20–21 October 2003. On some nights (26–27 September 2000 and 29–30 October 2003), nearly all detections

were birds (93% and 94%, respectively). Overall, we detected few foraging bats (26 of 1316 detections, or 2%).

At night, most migrating birds were 240– 800 m above ground (Fig. 3A), with a maximum altitude of 1500 m. Most insects detected were below 60 m. Rarely, some detections appeared in the radar beam and not the TI and these may have been insects too high to be seen in the TI, but reflective enough to produce an echo in the radar beam. Most detections of foraging bats were below 500 m and the highest was at 1343 m (Fig. 3C).

The maximum MTR during our nocturnal samples was on 26–27 September 2000 when detections indicated that 123,233 birds crossed a 1609.34 m front per hour during the first sample period (Table 2). Only on two evenings (29–30 October and 31 October–1 November 2003) were all birds in our samples flying above 60 m. On one evening (16–17 October 2003), only one bird was detected in the radar beam during two 5-min samples and it was below 60 m. The single bird at low altitude represented a MTR of 3199 birds per 1609.34 m of front per hour (Table 2).

The flight directions of birds and insects detected in the TI and vertical radar beam on the evening of 26–27 September 2000 are provided in Table 3. The lengths of the mean vectors for migrating birds were high and correspond to rather tight concentration around the mean.

Targets classified as insects moved toward a mean direction of 247[◦] and 256[◦] during the first 2 h and then shifted toward 241[◦] during the third hour when the angular variance increased. The flight paths of foraging bats were highly erratic and are not included in Table 3.

**Daytime monitoring, spring 2003.** Figure 4A is a 30-s time exposure from the VPS showing two flocks moving north, with one 185 m above the radar and the other 1158 m above radar level (arl). The tracks of 13 individual birds in the lower flock are visible and some birds were clearly changing position in the flock. Because the flock was near the edge of the field of view, the number of birds in the flock was unknown. Tracks of the six individual birds in the higher flock are hard to see because of the altitude of the flock (Fig. 4A), but some individuals were also changing position in the flock. The tracks in the higher flock are more evident when the VPS clip is being generated from the video and when enhanced in contrast and brightness through image processing (Fig. 4B). Two insect tracks (middlerighttoupperleft)arealsovisibleineach image. One of these was moving from WSW to ENE (upper) and the other from ENE to WSW (lower). Both were too low to be detected apart from the ground echo in the vertical radar beam.

We detected more birds than insects during 3 h of daytime observation on 1 May 2003 (Table 1). During the first hour, 60% of all detections were birds. Two hours later (closer to the peak arrival time of the flight), the proportion of birds was 96%. Most insect detections were below 60 m and most trans-Gulf migrants were above 120 m. Figure 3B shows the altitudinal distribution of birds detected in the TI and in the vertical radar beam. Although many birds were 120–960 m arl, the largest flocks of transGulf migrants were 1300–2130 m arl. Many detections represented individual birds (70 of 1054, or 6.6%), but 80 detections were flocks of two or more birds (mean flock size = 12.3 ± 11.5 [SD] birds, range = 2–50).

Bird MTRs for arriving trans-Gulf migration on 1 May 2003 increased from 54,181 birds per 1609.34 m of front for the first hour to 56,132 for the second hour and 108,188 for the third hour of sampling (Table 2). The flight directions of the insects were toward the WNW and NW, as were surface winds during the observations (winds from ESE and SSE at 7 m/s; Table 3). The flight directions of the trans-Gulf migrants were oriented between 6.7[◦] and 9.9[◦] and the circular standard deviation was considerable less than that for insects (Table 3). As the density of arriving transGulf migration increased, the circular standard deviation decreased. The winds at the 925-mb pressure level (762 m above ground level [agl]) were calm and, at the 850-mb pressure level (1457 m agl), were from the west at 6.5 m/s.

## **DISCUSSION**

The VERTRAD/TI combination represents a valuable tool for use during day or night. The TI, unlike the ceilometer beam technique (Gauthreaux 1969), requires no illumination for target detection, eliminating possible effects of illumination on the behavior of the birds, bats, and insects. The system works best under cloudless conditions because heat from clouds can obscure heat return from birds. The greatest altitude at which individual birds in a flock were resolved in our TI was 2871 m arl. Liechti et al. (1995) found that even small nocturnal migrants 3 km away were detected crossing the field of a

passive IR device. This difference in detection range can be attributed to the diameter of the parabolic antenna and the power of the radar (5 kW) we used for the VERTRAD. On several occasions, the TI detected targets we believed were high flying birds not detected by the vertical radar. We believe that more powerful radar (e.g., 25 or 50 kW) will solve this problem. The orientation of the system need not be vertical. Once collimated, the radar and thermal camera could be directed at any angle between horizontal and vertical.

Although Liechti et al (1995) found that the sizes of the thermal signature from birds in the field of a TI were roughly correlated to the distance of the birds measured with tracking radar, we believe that the use of the size of the thermal signature in the field of view of the TI to estimate the heights of migrants (Zehnder et al. 2001) can produce erroneous measures. The use of a fixed-beam vertically pointing radar (of sufficient power) and a vertically pointing TI eliminates such errors and allows more accurate measures of altitude needed to accurately determine MTRs.

Identifying sources of radar echoes in a radar display is difficult and usually requires visual confirmation. The TI and VPS combination makes identification easier because the VPS generates a time exposure image of the thermal radiance of a target. Characteristics of the track of the target can be used to identify the type of

organism. Insects have relatively weak thermal radiance and appear small at relatively low altitudes. Even a large insect produces less than 10 times the heat of a small bird (Zehnder et al. 2001). Small targets moving fast (fractions of a second) through the TI and not detected by the radar can be regarded as insects. Although birdsandbatsproducehighthermalradiance,we suspect that nonforaging, migrating bats could be confused with migrating birds that have a constant wing beat. Most bats did not produce VPS tracks that showed modulation from wing beat pattern, possibly because they were flying slowly. Foraging bats were identified mainly on the basis of their high radiance and irregular flight paths. Wing beat patterns of flying birds clearly produce modulations in the VPS tracks generated from video clips of the TI and produce pulsations of echoes in the radar beam. In the future, these patterns may be useful in identifying the type of bird detected.

The use of the TI also allows investigators to determine if an echo in the radar beam is produced by a single bird or a flock of birds. The VERTRAD/TI combination readily detected the arrival of trans-Gulf migrants during daylight and, because many species arrive in flocks during the day (Gauthreaux 1972), the TI was particularly useful in detecting individual

A limitation of TI cameras is their cost. In general, cooled thermal cameras are more expensive than uncooled ones. The cost of a cooled highresolution, high-sensitivity TI currently ranges from $35,000 to $50,000. The thermal camera used in our study cost about $60,000 in 1996. Another cautionary note concerns the equipment settings. The radar display should have the proper brightness and contrast levels so that echoes in the radar beam are clearly visible when the radar screen is being video recorded. This can also be affected by ambient lighting.

In a few cases (1 or 2 per 100 detections), we recorded an echo in the vertical radar beam, but saw nothing in the TI. One possible explanation is that large targets just outside the radar beam and the visual field of the TI could produce a weak radar echo because the width of the radar beam is determined by the 1/2 power point (3 dB drop in power), and a strong target not “in the beam” could reflect enough energy back to produce a weak echo. Another possibility is that the radar detects small targets, but the TI cannot

resolve them because of their size and altitude. This is what would be expected for high-flying small insects.

The vertically pointing, fixed-beam of the VERTRAD provided data about the altitude of most targets detected in the TI. The beam width of the VERTRAD was 4.0[◦] , and when the beam was collimated to the TI and centered in the middle of the visual field of the TI, it covered the vertical dimension of the viewing screen, but not the horizontal dimension. Thus, the TI detected more targets than the radar beam at a given altitude.

The altitudes of birds at night were typically lower than during the day, as also noted by Gauthreaux (1972). VERTRAD cannot detect flying birds below 25 m agl so it is not possible to accurately estimate the extent to which birds migrate in this altitudinal band. It is possible to compute a crude MTR using TI data below 25 m, but because the sampling volume is extremely small, more samples or samples of longer duration are needed, unless, of course, the number of birds moving within the stratum is very high. Above 25 m, each bird is associated with a particular altitude, permitting determination of how much nocturnal (and daytime) migration occurs within different altitudinal strata. Such data could be used to estimate the potential risk of migrating birds colliding with man-made structures of various heights (e.g., communicationandbroadcasttowersandwindturbines)—a subject of increasing importance to conservation biologists.
